stem: A 50-year-old man with disseminated tuberculosis presents with hypotension and shock, with pigmentation of the buccal mucosa and palmar creases. The biochemical abnormality most likely to be present is:
explanation: Adrenal insufficiency (TB Addison's) causes hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia.

stem: A 24-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with confusion after days of vomiting and diarrhoea. BP is low and he has hyperpigmented skin, most prominent on the hands. Na 124 mmol/l, K 6.6 mmol/l. The likely diagnosis is:
explanation: Hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypotension and pigmentation indicate Addison's disease with crisis.

stem: A patient has weakness and lethargy. BP is 100/60 mmHg, dropping to 80/40 mmHg on standing, and his skin is hyperpigmented. Which investigation helps to diagnose this case?
explanation: Postural hypotension with pigmentation suggests Addison's disease, which is confirmed by cortisol (with the short synacthen test); electrolytes only support it.
key_note: One paper key marked serum electrolytes; correct is serum cortisol. The stem's skin finding was an unreadable picture and is described as hyperpigmented by the reviewer.

stem: A 62-year-old woman has nausea, lethargy and abdominal pain, increased pigmentation of the buccal mucosa, hyperkalaemia and hyponatraemia. Which is the best investigation to confirm the suspected diagnosis of Addison's disease?

options.D: Oral glucose tolerance test with GH measurements

explanation: The short synacthen test shows failure of cortisol to rise and confirms adrenal insufficiency.

stem: A 40-year-old woman is diagnosed with Addison's disease. What combination of medications is she most likely to be prescribed?
explanation: Primary adrenal failure needs both glucocorticoid (hydrocortisone) and mineralocorticoid (fludrocortisone) replacement.
key_note: Not marked in the source paper; answer by reviewer.

stem: Which statement best describes an Addisonian crisis?

options.B: Severe adrenal insufficiency with dangerously low serum cortisol levels
options.C: Severe adrenal insufficiency with dangerously low serum testosterone levels

explanation: Addisonian (adrenal) crisis is acute cortisol deficiency with shock, hypoglycaemia and electrolyte disturbance.

stem: Features of acute adrenal crisis include all EXCEPT:
explanation: Adrenal crisis causes hypotension and shock, not hypertension.

stem: All of the following are causes of spontaneous hypoglycaemia EXCEPT:
explanation: Hypoglycaemia occurs with insulinoma, autoimmune insulin syndromes, liver failure and adrenal insufficiency; hypertension is not a cause.
key_note: Stem reworded: the source ('causes include') had four true options and the paper key D (Addison's) was one of them, so the only false option, primary hypertension, is the answer.

stem: A 30-year-old man presents with coarsening of facial features; he often changes shoe size and his ring no longer fits. Which feature is observed in this disease?
explanation: Acromegaly causes prognathism, frontal bossing and enlarged hands and feet.

stem: Which statement is NOT true about growth hormone therapy in adult hypopituitarism?

options.A: It is usually not given to adults as the epiphyses are closed
options.B: It can be given to adults incapacitated by lethargy
options.C: It is given as part of full hormone replacement therapy for pituitary failure
options.D: It is used as an aphrodisiac in adults

explanation: GH has no role as an aphrodisiac; replacement is selective for adults with severe GH deficiency and poor quality of life.

stem: A 60-year-old man has had repeated courses of oral prednisolone for exacerbations of COPD. Which adverse effect is linked to long-term steroid use?
explanation: Long-term glucocorticoids cause avascular necrosis of bone (femoral head) and osteoporosis; they raise, not lower, the white count.

stem: Which of the following results establishes a diagnosis of diabetes mellitus?

options.B: Asymptomatic patient with fasting glucose 140 mg/dl on one occasion
options.C: Symptomatic patient with fasting glucose of 140 mg/dl on one occasion
options.D: Asymptomatic patient with random glucose 220 mg/dl on one occasion
options.E: Symptomatic patient with random glucose 150 mg/dl on one occasion

explanation: A symptomatic patient needs only one abnormal value (fasting 126 mg/dl or more, or random 200 mg/dl or more). An asymptomatic patient needs the abnormal result confirmed on a second occasion, and glycosuria alone is never diagnostic.

stem: A 50-year-old woman complains of nocturia and increased thirst for a month. She has been losing weight recently. Urinalysis shows glycosuria and a random blood glucose level is elevated. What is the most likely underlying cause?
explanation: Polyuria, polydipsia and weight loss with glycosuria and raised random glucose is diabetes mellitus. Diabetes insipidus gives dilute urine without glycosuria.

stem: All of the following statements are correct about type 1 diabetes EXCEPT:

options.A: There is absolute deficiency of insulin
options.C: If not treated the patient can develop diabetic ketoacidosis
options.D: Type 1 diabetics are treated with oral drugs
options.E: Type 1 diabetes patients are usually thin

explanation: Type 1 diabetes is autoimmune beta-cell destruction with absolute insulin deficiency, so lifelong insulin is required; oral hypoglycaemic drugs do not work.

stem: All of the following statements are correct about type 2 diabetes EXCEPT:

options.A: There is relative insulin deficiency and insulin resistance
options.B: The patient presents in early childhood
options.C: Patients are usually obese (BMI more than 25)
options.D: Treatment usually consists of lifestyle modification and drugs
options.E: If not treated the patient can develop hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state

explanation: Type 2 diabetes classically presents in adulthood (though rising in obese adolescents); presentation in early childhood is typical of type 1.

stem: A 45-year-old type 2 diabetic presents for annual check-up. Which of the following is a microvascular complication of diabetes mellitus?

options.D: Digital gangrene due to peripheral vascular disease
options.E: Pain in the lower limb due to ischaemia

explanation: Microvascular complications are retinopathy, nephropathy and neuropathy. Stroke, MI and peripheral vascular disease are macrovascular.

stem: A 60-year-old obese man presents for a routine check-up. His fasting blood glucose is 130 mg/dl. He reports feeling more fatigued than usual and has noticed increased thirst and urination. What is the most appropriate initial management strategy for this patient?
explanation: Obese newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes with only modestly raised glucose is managed first with diet, weight loss and exercise; drugs (metformin) are added if targets are not met.
key_note: One paper key marked D (oral hypoglycaemic agents); two copies marked B, which is kept as the first step.

stem: A 65-year-old man has recently had blood tests. His HbA1c is 6.6% and his fasting blood glucose is 127 mg/dl. What is the most appropriate management?

options.D: Advise daily exercise and dietary modification

explanation: HbA1c of 6.5% or more with fasting glucose of 126 mg/dl or more confirms diabetes; metformin is the first-line drug alongside lifestyle advice.
key_note: Option D (lifestyle alone) is also acceptable as the first step in some teaching; the paper key A is kept.

stem: An overweight 68-year-old woman with a five-year history of type 2 diabetes attends for annual review. She is on metformin (2 g daily). Investigations reveal HbA1c 11.2%, raised serum creatinine and raised total cholesterol. Which is the most appropriate therapeutic option?

options.B: Start gliclazide in addition to metformin

explanation: HbA1c of 11.2% despite maximal metformin needs insulin, and the raised creatinine (renal impairment) makes continuing metformin unsafe because of lactic acidosis risk.
key_note: One paper key marked D (continue metformin); with raised creatinine, E is preferred.

stem: A 70-year-old diabetic lady has well-controlled blood sugar, but her relatives are concerned about frequent hypoglycaemic episodes. Which of the following drugs might she be taking?
explanation: Sulphonylureas such as gliclazide stimulate insulin secretion irrespective of glucose and are the oral drugs most often causing hypoglycaemia, especially in the elderly. The others rarely cause it alone.

stem: When starting a diabetic on insulin, which of the following advice regarding complications is correct?

options.A: Fasting blood glucose should be between 50 and 90 mg/dl
options.B: Abscesses at injection sites are a common side-effect
options.C: Night-time hypoglycaemia may present with poor sleep quality
options.D: Hyperglycaemia is the most common complication
options.E: HbA1c should be measured every week

explanation: Nocturnal hypoglycaemia causes restless sleep, night sweats, nightmares and morning headache. Hypoglycaemia (not hyperglycaemia) is the commonest complication of insulin, targets are not 50-90 mg/dl, and HbA1c is checked every 3 months.
key_note: Options D and E were merged in the source and have been separated by reviewer.

stem: A 30-year-old man with diabetes reports episodes of hypoglycaemia, especially after exercise, for the last month. His fasting insulin level is elevated while his C-peptide level is low. What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
explanation: High insulin with low C-peptide means the insulin is exogenous and the patient's own beta cells are not working, as in type 1 diabetes treated with injected insulin; insulinoma raises both insulin and C-peptide.
key_note: Question is flawed (option E, exogenous insulin, is biochemically similar); the paper keys all marked D, which is kept.

stem: A 50-year-old diabetic patient comes to the emergency department with generalised weakness and ill health. His blood sugar is 550 mg/dl. What is the recommended management?

options.A: Maintain I/V line with dextrose water

explanation: Severe hyperglycaemia in an unwell patient is a hyperglycaemic emergency needing IV fluids and a short-acting (soluble) insulin infusion. Dextrose, steroids and SGLT-2 inhibitors worsen or do not treat it.

stem: A 45-year-old patient with type 2 diabetes presents with acute onset chest pain and palpitations for 2 hours. His blood glucose is significantly elevated and serum insulin is undetectable. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
explanation: In a hyperglycaemic crisis with insulin deficiency (DKA picture), the first step is IV fluid resuscitation (normal saline); insulin follows once fluids and potassium status are addressed.
key_note: Paper keys differ (B marked in two copies, E circled in one); E is the first step per DKA protocol.

stem: A 35-year-old Lady Health Worker with diabetic ketoacidosis is admitted with serum glucose 412 mg/dl (22.9 mmol/L), pH 7.12, K 4.4 mEq/L, Na 141 mEq/L. Which of the following is the appropriate initial treatment?

options.A: Hypotonic sodium chloride (0.45%) solution and insulin
options.D: Normal saline, potassium, insulin and bicarbonate

explanation: DKA is treated with isotonic saline and insulin infusion, and potassium is added to the fluids when serum K is below about 5.3 mEq/L (here 4.4) because insulin drives K into cells. Bicarbonate is only for pH below 6.9.
key_note: Not marked in the source paper; answer by reviewer.

stem: A 17-year-old female presents with severe abdominal pain and vomiting for 2 days. She is tachypnoeic and her breath has a fruity odour. Random blood sugar is 600 mg/dl. ABG: pH 7.15, pCO2 31 mmHg, HCO3 11.9 mEq/l, pO2 79 mmHg. Serum Na 141, K 4.26, Cl 100 mEq/l. What is the primary abnormality?
explanation: Anion gap = 141 - (100 + 11.9) = about 29 (normal 8-12), with low pH and low bicarbonate: high anion gap metabolic acidosis from ketoacids in DKA; the low pCO2 is respiratory compensation.

stem: A 21-year-old known type 1 diabetic presents with abdominal pain and vomiting for 1 day. BSR is 460 mg/dl and DKA is suspected and treated. Which complication can he develop during treatment?
explanation: Cerebral oedema is the feared complication of DKA treatment (especially in the young) from rapid fall in glucose and osmolality; other complications include hypokalaemia and hypoglycaemia.

stem: A 40-year-old woman complains of severe fatigue, weight loss and irregular menstrual cycles for 1 month. She has a family history of autoimmune diseases. Laboratory findings show elevated anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Raised anti-TPO antibodies with a family history of autoimmunity points to Hashimoto's thyroiditis.

stem: A 50-year-old lady presents to OPD with weight gain. Her thyroid function tests show low T3, low T4 and low TSH. The most likely diagnosis is:
explanation: Low thyroid hormones with a low (not raised) TSH indicates pituitary (central, secondary) hypothyroidism; in primary hypothyroidism TSH is high.

stem: A 75-year-old man presents with malaise, weight loss and anorexia. He has rapid atrial fibrillation and leg oedema. Which one of the following diagnoses is consistent with this picture?
explanation: Apathetic thyrotoxicosis in the elderly presents with weight loss, atrial fibrillation and heart failure rather than classical hyperactivity.

stem: A young woman presents with goitre. She is diagnosed with Graves' disease on the basis of eye signs and positive thyrotropin receptor antibody (TRAb). Which of the following is part of the syndrome?
explanation: Pretibial myxoedema (thyroid dermopathy), ophthalmopathy and acropachy are the extrathyroidal features specific to Graves' disease; the other options are features of hypothyroidism.

stem: A 40-year-old woman has an 8-month history of constant sweating and occasional feverishness. She has lost weight though her appetite is good. She is afebrile but tachycardic with sweaty palms. No goitre or cervical lymphadenopathy. Routine labs are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Sweating, weight loss despite good appetite, tachycardia and warm sweaty palms indicate thyrotoxicosis, which can occur without a palpable goitre. Check TSH and free T4.

stem: A 25-year-old patient presents with palpitations, anxiety and heat intolerance for 2 months. She has a small, smooth goitre, pulse 88/min, fine tremor and sweaty palms. TSH is <0.01, T4 and T3 elevated. Thyroid scan shows uniformly increased uptake of technetium. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Diffuse smooth goitre with diffusely increased uptake is Graves' disease; toxic adenoma and multinodular goitre show focal (patchy) uptake and thyroiditis shows low uptake.

stem: A 40-year-old female presents with palpitations and sweaty palms. Labs show high T4 and low TSH. Radioactive iodine uptake shows generalised low uptake. The most likely cause is:
explanation: Thyrotoxicosis with low radioiodine uptake means hormone is leaking from a damaged gland (thyroiditis) rather than being overproduced, as in Graves' or toxic nodular disease.

stem: A 29-year-old woman with a 10-month-old baby presents with neck and throat pain a week after a flu-like illness. The thyroid is mildly enlarged and tender. She has a slight tremor. Investigations show low TSH, raised free T4 and decreased radioiodine uptake. Which form of thyroiditis is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A painful tender goitre after a viral illness with thyrotoxicosis and low uptake is subacute (De Quervain's) granulomatous thyroiditis. Postpartum thyroiditis is painless.

stem: A 32-year-old woman, 24 weeks pregnant, has symptoms of an upper respiratory tract infection and pain over the thyroid for 5 days, with generalised tenderness of the gland, anxiety and palpitations. Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?
explanation: This is subacute thyroiditis: treat pain with NSAIDs, with a beta-blocker for symptoms; antithyroid drugs do not work because there is no hormone overproduction, and steroids are reserved for severe cases.

stem: A 20-year-old female presents with a 2-week history of palpitations and tremors. There is a small diffusely enlarged goitre. The mainstay of treatment is:
explanation: Thionamides, chiefly carbimazole, are the mainstay of medical treatment of Graves' thyrotoxicosis. Propylthiouracil is second line (first trimester of pregnancy, thyroid storm, carbimazole reaction).
key_note: Paper key marked D (propylthiouracil); carbimazole is first-line, so A is correct.

stem: A 42-year-old woman presents with anxiety for 3 months, weight loss and palpitations. She was previously prescribed an SSRI without benefit. She has a fine tremor and pulse 88/min. Thyroid function tests show low TSH and raised T3 and T4. What is the appropriate therapy?
explanation: This is primary thyrotoxicosis (probably Graves'), so an antithyroid drug such as carbimazole is the appropriate treatment; propranolol only gives symptom relief.

stem: A 23-year-old woman who is 10 weeks pregnant has tiredness and morning sickness. Her TSH is borderline low and free T4 is mildly raised. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.B: Repeat thyroid function tests after 2 weeks

explanation: Slightly low TSH and mildly raised free T4 in early pregnancy is usually physiological from hCG stimulation of the TSH receptor (gestational transient thyrotoxicosis), so repeat the tests before treating; radioiodine is contraindicated.
key_note: One paper key marked D (propylthiouracil); in the variant with reordered options, repeat after 2 weeks was circled. Repeat TFTs is correct for this mild picture.

stem: A 34-year-old woman presents with sore throat and anal pain after starting medical treatment for Graves' disease. What investigation would you order?
explanation: Sore throat or mouth ulcers on carbimazole suggests agranulocytosis; stop the drug and send an urgent full blood count with differential.

stem: A 50-year-old woman with Graves' disease on propranolol and carbimazole complains of sore eyes and double vision at extremes of gaze. There is marked proptosis. Artificial tears and eye patches have not helped. Which is the initial treatment of choice to improve the ophthalmopathy?
explanation: Active moderate to severe Graves' orbitopathy is treated first with high-dose IV methylprednisolone; radiotherapy and decompression are second-line, and radioiodine can worsen the eyes.

stem: A 45-year-old woman has a 2.5 cm solitary thyroid nodule with no tenderness or lymphadenopathy. TSH is normal. Ultrasound shows a hypoechoic solid nodule with microcalcifications and irregular margins. What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.D: Observe and repeat ultrasound in one year

explanation: A solitary nodule with suspicious ultrasound features and normal TSH needs ultrasound-guided FNAC to exclude papillary carcinoma.

stem: A 36-year-old man has a firm thyroid nodule and chronic diarrhoea, with mucosal neuromas on the tongue and marfanoid features. Serum calcitonin is elevated and a cousin had pheochromocytoma. What is the single most likely tumour type?
explanation: Raised calcitonin from parafollicular C cells with mucosal neuromas and marfanoid habitus is medullary carcinoma in MEN 2B (RET mutation).

stem: A 40-year-old male is investigated for shortness of breath and stridor. His Pemberton sign is positive. This sign is used to demonstrate which disease?
explanation: Pemberton's sign is facial congestion and distended neck veins on raising both arms above the head, from thoracic inlet obstruction by a retrosternal goitre.
key_note: Sign name was missing in the source; supplied by reviewer from the answer.

stem: A 43-year-old woman complains of feeling weak all the time, 9 months after finishing pulmonary tuberculosis treatment. She is tanned and has postural hypotension. Which one of the following would cast doubt upon your provisional diagnosis?
explanation: The provisional diagnosis is Addison's disease (tuberculous adrenalitis), which causes hyperkalaemia and hyponatraemia; hypokalaemia would argue against it.

stem: A medical student presents with generalised pigmentation especially of flexural surfaces and palmar creases, weakness and easy fatigability, and buccal pigmentation. Na 133 mmol/L, K 5.5 mmol/L. The probable diagnosis is:
explanation: Pigmentation of creases and mucosa with hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia is primary adrenal insufficiency (raised ACTH and related peptides stimulate melanocytes).

stem: A 56-year-old man presents with unintentional weight loss and tiredness. He has hyperpigmented skin and BP 90/60 mmHg. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation: Weight loss, fatigue, hypotension and hyperpigmentation point to Addison's disease.

stem: A patient presents with extreme lethargy for a few months and two fits before reaching the ER. He has hyperpigmented hands and is emaciated. JVP is not raised, chest is clear and he is not dehydrated. Serum Na is 115 mEq/l. What can be the cause of the hyponatraemia?
explanation: Pigmentation, emaciation and severe hyponatraemia point to adrenal insufficiency, where cortisol lack impairs water excretion and aldosterone lack causes sodium loss.

stem: Which one of the following is NOT a feature of Addison's disease?
explanation: Addison's disease causes weight loss and anorexia, not weight gain.

stem: A 75-year-old man presents to the emergency department with severe hypotension and confusion. He has hypertension and type 2 diabetes. Tests show elevated ACTH and low cortisol levels. What condition does he likely have?
explanation: Low cortisol with high ACTH means the adrenal gland itself has failed (primary adrenal insufficiency); in secondary insufficiency ACTH is low.

stem: Which of the following skin changes is seen as a side effect of steroid administration?
explanation: Glucocorticoids cause skin atrophy and thinning with easy bruising and striae through loss of collagen.

stem: A man presents with weight gain, purple abdominal striae, thin hair and skin, and proximal muscle weakness. BP is 180/110 mmHg. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation: Central weight gain, purple striae, skin thinning, proximal myopathy and hypertension are the classical features of Cushing's syndrome.

stem: A 45-year-old woman has fatigue for 2 months, central obesity, a round face and purple abdominal striae. Serum cortisol is raised and not suppressed by a low-dose dexamethasone suppression test. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Cortisol that fails to suppress on low-dose dexamethasone confirms endogenous Cushing's syndrome.

stem: A 47-year-old woman has progressive central weight gain, easy bruising, proximal myopathy, purple abdominal striae, facial plethora and hypertension. Cushing's syndrome is suspected. Which is the single most appropriate initial screening test?
explanation: Initial screening is the overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test, 24-hour urinary free cortisol or late-night salivary cortisol; localisation (ACTH, MRI) follows confirmation.

stem: A suspected case of Cushing's syndrome is seen in OPD. After baseline labs, which imaging would you preferably perform to localise the lesion?
explanation: Pituitary adenoma (Cushing's disease) is the commonest endogenous cause, so MRI of the pituitary is the usual first localising study once ACTH-dependence is shown.

stem: A 35-year-old man, a known case of pulmonary TB, presents in the ER with dizziness and a fall, and a significant postural drop in blood pressure. Investigations: pH 7.28, PaCO2 32 mmHg, HCO3 16 mmol/L, anion gap 10 mmol/L. What is the likely acid-base disorder?
explanation: Low pH and low bicarbonate with a normal anion gap is a normal anion gap (hyperchloraemic) metabolic acidosis; here it is explained by hypoaldosteronism from tuberculous Addison's disease.
key_note: The second copy's lab values were missing in the source; the key is the same.

stem: A 42-year-old woman has difficult-to-control hypertension despite three agents; BP 170/104 mmHg with no Cushingoid features. Investigations show persistent hypokalaemia with metabolic alkalosis and suppressed plasma renin. What is the single most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Resistant hypertension with hypokalaemic alkalosis and suppressed renin is primary aldosteronism; renal artery stenosis would give high renin.

stem: A patient presents with intermittent episodes of headache, palpitations and sweating for several months. On examination she is anxious, pulse is 100/min and BP is 170/100 mmHg (episodic severe hypertension). What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The triad of episodic headache, palpitations and sweating with paroxysmal hypertension is the classical presentation of pheochromocytoma (catecholamine excess).
key_note: Merged from two papers with slightly different distractors; both keys agree on pheochromocytoma.

stem: A 43-year-old man has episodic pounding headaches, palpitations and profuse sweating. During attacks BP is 210/110 mmHg and he is anxious and tremulous. Urinary metanephrines and normetanephrines are markedly elevated. What is the single most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Raised urinary metanephrines confirm pheochromocytoma.

stem: A 50-year-old male presents with progressive enlargement of his hands, feet and jaw for 4 months, with joint pain and headaches. Lab findings show elevated IGF-1 and failure to suppress GH on oral glucose tolerance testing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Enlargement of the extremities and jaw with raised IGF-1 and non-suppressible GH on OGTT is acromegaly from a GH-secreting pituitary adenoma.

stem: A 16-year-old boy is brought because of excessive height. He has large hands, a prominent lower jaw and excessive sweating. His growth hormone is raised and not suppressed on OGTT. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: GH excess before epiphyseal closure causes gigantism (tall stature with acromegalic features); Marfan's syndrome has normal GH and normal sweating.

stem: A 36-year-old man complains of loss of libido and impotence. Serum prolactin is 3200 mU/l (normal <360) and testosterone is low. There is no visual field disturbance. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A markedly raised prolactin in a man with hypogonadism and no visual field defect is a prolactinoma, and a level of about 3000 mU/l with no mass effect fits a microadenoma (macroadenomas usually give higher levels with visual symptoms). Stalk compression gives only modest rises.
key_note: Defensible either way; the paper key (E) is kept.

stem: A 50-year-old woman presents with polyuria and polydipsia following recent transsphenoidal surgery. The biochemical abnormality that correlates best with this condition is:
explanation: Post-pituitary surgery cranial diabetes insipidus causes water loss with high plasma osmolality, high serum sodium and dilute urine.

stem: A 36-year-old female at 36 weeks of pregnancy has heavy blood loss (placental abruption and caesarean section). She later cannot produce milk and feels fatigued, and Sheehan syndrome is suspected. Which anatomical structure has infarcted?
explanation: Sheehan syndrome is postpartum pituitary necrosis from haemorrhage and hypotension, since the enlarged pregnant pituitary is vulnerable; the first sign is failure of lactation.

stem: A 30-year-old woman presents six months after a massive postpartum haemorrhage with fatigue, failure to lactate, amenorrhoea and cold intolerance. BP is low and axillary hair is lost. Free T4 is low with inappropriately low or normal TSH, and morning cortisol is low. What is the single most likely diagnosis?

options.B: Adrenal insufficiency due to autoimmune Addison's

explanation: Multiple pituitary hormone deficits (low T4 with non-raised TSH, low cortisol, failure of lactation, amenorrhoea) after postpartum haemorrhage indicate Sheehan syndrome.

stem: A 28-year-old abnormally tall athlete presents with decreased libido, fatigue and gynaecomastia for a month. Tests show low testosterone and elevated oestradiol. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Tall stature, gynaecomastia and hypogonadism with low testosterone and raised oestradiol (and raised FSH/LH) is Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY).

stem: A 12-year-old girl is brought for delayed puberty. She has minimal breast development. FSH, LH and oestrogen levels are all normal. What is the most likely cause?

options.B: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty

explanation: Normal gonadotrophins and oestrogen for a prepubertal state point to constitutional delay, which resolves spontaneously. Primary ovarian insufficiency and Turner syndrome give high FSH/LH.
key_note: Two copies were marked A (androgen insensitivity) and one B; AIS gives high LH and testosterone with normal breasts and primary amenorrhoea, so B is correct.

stem: A 40-year-old woman is evaluated for infertility. She has a BMI of 30 and her serum progesterone is low, suggesting anovulation. What is the most appropriate first step in management?
explanation: In obese anovulatory women, weight loss restores ovulation in many cases and is the first step before ovulation induction.

stem: A 22-year-old overweight woman (BMI 32 kg/m2) has acne and hirsutism of the face and upper chest, and periods only every 3 to 4 months. Investigations show raised gonadotrophin and serum testosterone. What is the most appropriate first-line management?
explanation: In PCOS with hirsutism, acne and oligomenorrhoea, the combined oral contraceptive pill is first-line (it regularises cycles and lowers androgens); weight loss is advised alongside.
key_note: Paper key (oral contraceptive pill) kept; weight loss is the usual lifestyle measure alongside.

stem: A 27-year-old woman has difficulty conceiving, is overweight and has acne and hirsutism. An ultrasound shows polycystic ovaries. Which hormone excess has caused the hirsutism?
explanation: Hirsutism results from excess androgens (testosterone) acting on hair follicles in polycystic ovary syndrome.

stem: A 26-year-old woman has oligomenorrhoea, hirsutism, acne and weight gain. BMI is 31 kg/m2 with acanthosis nigricans. Free testosterone is mildly elevated and ultrasound shows multiple peripheral follicles. What is the single most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Oligomenorrhoea, hyperandrogenism, insulin resistance (acanthosis) and polycystic ovaries fit PCOS (Rotterdam criteria); a tumour gives rapid virilisation and very high testosterone.
key_note: The testosterone value was garbled in the source; stem wording by reviewer.

stem: A 65-year-old female presents with frequent fractures, fatigue and kidney stones for 1 year. Labs show hypercalcaemia, low phosphate and elevated PTH. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: High calcium with low phosphate and raised PTH is primary hyperparathyroidism: bones, stones, abdominal groans and psychic moans.

stem: A 45-year-old man is diagnosed with primary hyperparathyroidism after elevated calcium and low phosphorus were found. Which symptoms might he exhibit?
explanation: Primary hyperparathyroidism causes bone pain (osteitis fibrosa cystica) and renal stones, along with constipation and neuropsychiatric symptoms.

stem: A 55-year-old woman with osteoporosis has an elevated PTH, while serum calcium and phosphorus are normal. What is the most likely cause of her osteoporosis?
explanation: Raised PTH with normal calcium indicates compensatory (secondary) hyperparathyroidism, for example from vitamin D deficiency; primary hyperparathyroidism is expected to raise calcium. Drug-induced and postmenopausal osteoporosis do not raise PTH.
key_note: The source copy marked A (drug-induced osteoporosis), which cannot explain a raised PTH; the stem is weak, answer by reviewer.

stem: A 52-year-old woman develops perioral tingling and carpopedal spasm two days after total thyroidectomy. Chvostek and Trousseau signs are positive. Labs show low calcium, high phosphate and low PTH. What is the single most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Low calcium, high phosphate and low PTH after thyroidectomy means accidental parathyroid removal or devascularisation. Pseudohypoparathyroidism has high PTH; hungry bone syndrome gives low phosphate.

stem: On World Osteoporosis Day, an audience member asks about the common site of osteoporotic fractures. The correct response is:
explanation: Vertebral (spine) fractures are the commonest osteoporotic fractures; hip and distal radius (Colles') fractures follow, but the hip carries the highest morbidity and mortality.
key_note: Paper key A (spine) kept; some sources stress the hip as the most important site.

stem: A post-menopausal woman with an abnormal bone mineral density test is diagnosed with osteoporosis. Which of the following is present in this condition?
explanation: Osteoporosis is reduced bone mass and density with normal mineralisation and microarchitectural deterioration (T-score -2.5 or below); osteomalacia is the condition with defective mineralisation.

stem: Which one of the following is least recognised as a risk factor for developing osteoporosis?
explanation: Hyperthyroidism (not hypothyroidism) accelerates bone loss; Cushing's, Turner's, hyperparathyroidism and diabetes are all recognised causes.

stem: The following are causes of BMI greater than 30 kg/m2 EXCEPT:
explanation: Obesity (BMI above 30) results from genetics, excess calorie intake and inactivity; smoking is associated with lower body weight.

stem: A 38-year-old woman has BMI 32 kg/m2, hypertension and raised LDL cholesterol, and wants to lose weight. What is the most effective initial strategy for weight management?
explanation: Diet, physical activity and behavioural change are the first-line foundation of obesity management; drugs and surgery are added only if this fails and BMI criteria are met.

stem: The metabolic syndrome includes:

options.A: Diabetes, ischaemic heart disease and obesity
options.D: Ischaemic heart disease, hypertension and dyslipidaemia

explanation: Metabolic syndrome is central obesity with insulin resistance or diabetes, plus hypertension and dyslipidaemia; of the options only diabetes, hypertension and obesity are components.

stem: Which of the following drugs is used to treat obesity pharmacologically in patients with BMI above 40?
explanation: Orlistat, a pancreatic lipase inhibitor that reduces fat absorption, is the anti-obesity drug in this list; the others cause weight gain or have no role.

stem: A 28-year-old woman, 10 weeks pregnant, is hypertensive at her booking visit. Blood and urine tests are normal except for a low potassium of 3.1 mmol/l. Which is the most likely cause?
explanation: Hypertension with hypokalaemia suggests primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome); pregnancy-induced hypertension occurs after 20 weeks.
